body_text: As companies like DoorDash , Uber and Amazon race to deliver packages and burritos via drones, an unlikely competitor is giving them a run for their money: a chimpanzee sanctuary in Florida . After heavy rains flooded the sanctuary's roads, staff turned to a drone to deliver food to Kaleb, a 38-year-old chimpanzee stranded by the rising waters. His order? Hims’ margins, not unlike many of its customers, are getting slimmer. Can peptides help it get back to profit growth? Both Eli Lilly and Novo (formerly known as Novo Nordisk ) reported sales numbers that beat estimates and hiked their outlooks. Earlier this year, both companies released oral GLP-1s that have by all accounts been flying off the pharmacy shelves without cannibalizing sales from its legacy injectable products. Over the years, Lilly and Novo have increasingly sold the drugs through direct-to-consumer channels, often through partnerships with telehealth companies like Hims & Hers. Hims used to sell knock-off versions of Novo’s injectable drugs, which were produced in compounding pharmacies (some owned by Hims, others through partnerships) and officially marketed as bespoke treatments. After more than a year of threats and a brief legal battle with Novo, Hims no longer sells those high-margin knock-offs. Now, it offers Novo and Lilly’s branded drugs on its platforms, which carry significantly lower margins. The company’s profits have taken a hit as a result. On Monday it reported a surprise loss for the quarter along with sales and subscriber count numbers that missed expectations. It also cut its outlook for the year. “We had, as you all saw in the last quarter or two, just a massive transformation of the business, moving from the compounding offerings to the partnership with Novo,” Hims CEO Andrew Dudum told analysts on Monday. Hims also said it will begin offering some unapproved peptide treatments this month after US regulators eased restrictions. Dudum said the new offering will include glutathione, NAD, sermorelin and B12, with BPC-157 and TB-500 potentially coming later, subject to regulatory approval. For the unacquainted, peptides are under-studied supplements , usually injectable, that have grown in popularity in recent years because of their purported health benefits. As of now, consumers are bypassing the FDA by buying vials of peptides labeled “for research use only” and then conducting that research on themselves. Importantly for Hims: the company can sell these treatments while controlling much of the supply chain, from manufacturing to distribution. While it’s unclear how big the market truly is, peptides could offer the kind of attractive margins Hims enjoyed when it was selling compounded GLP-1s. Hims has already acquired a peptide manufacturing facility in Menlo Park, California, and says it's seen a “tremendous amount of excitement” from customers on its waitlist, per Dudum. But the company isn't expecting the new business to contribute meaningfully to revenue in the current quarter. Hims does best when it behaves like a drugmaker , selling its own products versus made in an industrial pharmacy rather than serving as the sleek, neutral colored liaison between you and an actual pharmaceutical company. Selling compounded GLP-1s was very lucrative for Hims. Peptides could give it another shot at that business model. But the company is once again betting on a category where the regulatory ground is still shifting beneath its feet. “In healthcare, whoever owns the customer relationship wins,” Dudum said. title: 👀 Affair valuation
body_text: The American consumer is exhausted and enraged by rising prices, and ready, according to consumer data, to spend a $1 billion on packaged food that’s labeled “seed-oil free.” Seed oils are, of course, the fashionable, if scientifically dubious, boogeyman. Data doesn’t back up claims of various health harms caused by seed oils but the Americans aren’t letting that get in the way: seed-oil-free products saw a 72% gain compared to a year earlier, and sales of seed-oil-free salty snacks climbed 87%, compared to just 2.9% for products without the label, Bloomberg News reported based on NIQ data. Big food companies like PepsiCo and ConAgra are making the switch by relying on olive and avocado oil. Markets bounced back Monday, rising after last week’s AI-trade induced wipeout, despite news over the weekend about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy (more on that story below.) “We’ve spent all this time worrying about AI cybersecurity risks when our true vulnerabilities come from human frailty,” was how Entrypoint’s Luke Kawa summed it up . On Sunday, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang released a statement admitting to an extra-marital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang’s statement comes after the New York Times first reported on the CEO’s “close” relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le. American officials, the NYT reported, had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset and involved in helping China evade constraints limiting its ability to import high-powered AI chips. Nvidia’s board of directors has opened an investigation into Huang’s conduct but has said it does not believe US national security or its own intellectual property have been compromised. The specifics don’t look good: Alice Huang is the CEO of Megaspeed , a Singapore-based data center company that has been an absolutely massive buyer of Nvidia chips. She is believed by US intelligence officials to have been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS), the Financial Times reported . The MSS fulfills a role similar to a combination of the CIA, FBI, and NSA. The US Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions that it was buying Nvidia AI chips in order to smuggle them into China before the probe was suddenly called off and transferred to the Justice Department late last year, the New York Times reported Monday . That switch came after Nvidia’s general counsel emailed Commerce Department investigators seeking information about the inquiry. Other tech stocks surged on Monday – the PHLX Semiconductor index gained almost 7% despite Nvdia falling about 4.5% on the day. As Kawa pointed out in yesterday’s Entrypoint newsletter, the market has for months now been a bit skeptical about the medium-term outlook for Nvdia’s profits. If you assume the chip giant’s quarter-on-quarter earnings-per-share growth dips to less than half its current average and investors give the stock a valuation in its recent lowest quartile, Kawa ballparks that Nvidia would be worth… about what it is today. Score one for the strong-form efficient markets hypothesis , I guess. At the same time, it’s hard exactly to know how Jensen Huang will respond to being put under a very new kind of public spotlight, and whether investors will have confidence in anyone but him to deliver the kind of returns he has overseen. title: 🎓 Midterms Studying
body_text: Sometimes it’s important to remember what sport you’re playing, as recently a hard-fought Brazilian youth soccer game devolved into a piqued MLB game or relatively subdued and reasonable ice hockey game. The game became a brawl that resulted in a world-record 53 red cards that ejected 43 players, 8 coaches, and two team board members from the fight on the field. In any company, it’s always nice to know the board has got your back, I guess. On Friday, stocks rebounded somewhat from Thursday’s $2.5T Nasdaq bloodbath, but overall finished a volatile week in the red. Last week the midterms resulted in a sweeping victory for congressional Democrats, and in the days that followed it became clear that what that means for the market is obvious, uncomplicated, and straightforward: nobody really knows exactly what that meant for the market, it’s very complicated and in no way straightforward. The day after the midterms stocks surged, the day after that the Nasdaq took a historic dump, and then the day after that things bounced back a bit. The upshot of last week in the aggregate was down a bit, but sector-by-sector things are not so simple. Companies used the opportunity of the market chaos to rip off some band-aids. Microsoft made a flurry of announcements that amounted to a paring back deals with the external providers of compute — chastising the neoclouds and pulling the plug on a compute rental provided by Oracle — that certainly sent a chill through the parts of the AI trade that serve those interests. Tesla managed to pop 5% on Friday in a week that was, electorally speaking, a fundamental rejection of the political project of Elon Musk. It did so by announcing that it was going to stop bleeding money out making Cybertrucks, and instead throw those production lines towards making Cybercabs. There was lots of more general house cleaning, such as Waymo announcing it would soon soon be done working with Uber , Oracle canceling a chip lease agreement with Tencent, Kraft Heinz planning to sell off its coffee business, and CVS spinning off… CVS. All the kind of news you drop when the market is so crazy you can’t really figure out what’s moving what. In all, the week was less about the end of this trade or the start of that, but more of a rotation. Hyperscalers Microsoft, Amazon and Google all finished the week up; if the week revealed anything, it’s that having existing datacenters in the ground is important, and that if you’re a company planning on putting more in the ground, well, maybe you should let Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa save you from yourself, and just go ahead and give that money to shareholders instead. Meanwhile, some of the biggest losers of the week were the companies that were riding the high of those companies capex moves. Some of the biggest drops of the week were storage chips ( Seagate , Sandisk ) and the connectivity and so-called “picks-and-shovels” of the data center build-out ( Lumentum , Marvell , Astera Labs , Micron ). Speaking of picks and shovels, another trade indicates how the midterms’ pushback on new data center construction has manifested in markets. Sure, companies like Caterpillar dropped, but homebuilders gained. Caterpillar supplies the literal picks and shovels of the data center build-out, and with that potentially slowing down, so did it. On the other hand, homebuilders that have had an exhausting time competing with data center construction for capital, materials, and labor surged, with Toll Brothers , DR Horton and PulteGroup all finishing the week up. A nota bene on PulteGroup that shows how weird this market has been. The large residential construction company was a huge winner of the week, spiking 8% between Tuesday's close and Wednesday's open, finishing the week up nearly 5%, now that Democrats will finally have a hand in steering housing policy. This is a somewhat ironic market rebuke of the administration, given that the grandson of the company's founder is currently serving as Trump's director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency and head of Freddie Mac. My colleague Luke Kawa, who writes the brilliant EntryPoint newsletter that goes in-depth on this stuff, is fond of the aphorism “my capex spending is your profit margins,” and that has been on display this past week. The AI trade will continue, but the beneficiaries of that trade — and the ultimate total addressable market of the business — will remain in flux. A few weeks ago, we wrote about the CoreWeave debt contretemps, and we made the point that just because a company got a lot of money doesn’t mean it’s gonna be one of the winners of the AI trade, writing “Just because your business model was the beating heart of the AI industry in 2026 doesn’t prevent you from being the bloated, doomed appendix of the AI industry in 2032. Not every buzzy well-funded company’s gonna make it.” Last week, if anything, confirmed that the future indeed won’t be evenly distributed.
